comparator.name: Bachelor Geneeskunde
comparator.academicYear: 2025-2026 (curriculum 2022; the most recent curriculum published on the official programme pages, which list course documents for 2023-2024 to 2025-2026 only; pages and catalogue checked 2026-10-01)
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from the official Maastricht University programme pages (s0 programme page, s1 Courses & curriculum, s2 Why this programme, s3 Your future) and the official Faculty of Health, Medicine and Life Sciences course catalogue for the bachelor Medicine 2025-2026 (s4). The bachelor Geneeskunde is a Dutch-language, numerus fixus, full-time three-year programme in Maastricht (curriculum 2022); the English-language track is discontinued from 2026-2027 (s5). The 2025-2026 curriculum is the most recent one that the official programme pages publish: the pages (checked 2026-10-01) list course documents for 2023-2024, 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 only, and the page for 2026-2027 courses was not available. Structure: years 1 and 2 each consist of four 10-week periods themed on health-care practice (Acute care, Short-term care, Chronic care, Preventive care / Care for health), followed in year 3 by a 20-week minor and a 20-week Integrated Care period; the three longitudinal tracks (Medical Professional, Critical Professional, Professional and Personal Development) run through all periods, and students follow elective education for about half a day per week and take part in a healthcare team in a regional care institution. EC are not published per period or per course: the catalogue gives 0 EC to every period and track and awards credit through annual competency exams, 60 EC in year 1 (MED1300), 60 EC in year 2 (MED2300) and 30 EC in year 3 (MED3300), with the 20-week minor listed at 30 EC (FHML minor Leefstijlgeneeskunde), which gives 60 + 60 + 30 + 30 = 180 EC. The four components therefore follow the official EC structure at the level at which it is published, and no EC are divided between periods. There are no formal routes or specialisations and no separate bachelor thesis. Course codes in the catalogue that carry a GEN prefix belong to the superseded earlier curriculum and are not used. Pages and document checked 2026-10-01.

components.name: Year 1: four 10-week care periods (Acute Care I, Short Term Care I, Chronic Care I, Care for Health) with the Medical Professional, Critical Professional and Personal & Professional Development tracks, electives and the Competency Exam Year 1
components.note: Compulsory. The official course catalogue (s4) assigns 0 EC to each period and track and awards the 60 EC of the year through the Competency Exam Year 1 (MED1300), so the year is kept as one component at its official EC weight; no EC split between periods is published or invented.

components.name: Year 2: four 10-week care periods (Short Term Care II, Acute Care II, Prevention, Chronic Care II) with the three longitudinal tracks, two electives, healthcare team participation and the Competency Exam Year 2
components.note: Compulsory. The catalogue (s4) awards the 60 EC of the year through the Competency Exam Year 2 (MED2300); the two electives and the 20-week healthcare team participation carry no separate EC. Patient contact in clinical settings begins in this year.

components.name: Year 3: minor period of 20 weeks (a minor at FHML or another UM faculty, study abroad or a free-mover period)
components.note: Open elective space. The 20-week minor is a free choice among FHML minors, minors at other UM faculties and study abroad; the catalogue (s4) lists 30 EC for the FHML minor Leefstijlgeneeskunde and the minor period covers half of the 40-week year. No named minor is instantiated.

components.name: Year 3: Integrated Care period of 20 weeks (Integrated Care 1 and 2) with the three longitudinal tracks, including Critical Appraisal of a Topic, and the Competency Exam Year 3
components.note: Compulsory. The catalogue (s4) awards 30 EC through the Competency Exam Year 3 (MED3300); the programme has no separate bachelor thesis, the research competency is assessed within the Critical Professional track.

programmes.label: Closest match to Medicine: Biomedical Science, Psychology and Evidence-Based Health Research
Health Psychology, Communication and Leadership for Patient-Centred Care

coreField.label: Biomedical knowledge base of the human body in health and disease: the body-system and care-themed periods of the programme (Acute Care with vital functions, circulation and respiration; Short Term Care; Chronic Care with the musculoskeletal and nervous systems) in which knowledge, skills and attitude are learned through authentic doctor tasks, and the programme's explicit aim to teach diagnosing health problems.
Treatment, pharmacotherapy and monitoring of patients: the programme's treating and monitoring competency as part of integrated care.
Prevention, epidemiology and the health of populations: the Care for Health / Prevention period of the curriculum, preventing disease and health problems that affect whole populations.

Scientific thinking, research methods, statistics and critical appraisal of evidence: the Critical Professional track (epidemiology, statistics including regression and logistic regression, bias assessment and meta-analysis, scientific writing, journal clubs, Cochrane systematic reviews, critical appraisal of a topic) and the scholar competency, with no separate bachelor thesis.

Ethics, law and professional responsibility: the ethics-and-law domain of the Critical Professional track (values, norms and rules governing medicine, health law and health ethics assignments, moral deliberation) and the programme's moral-ethical reasoning and professionalism.

Biopsychosocial and mental-health perspective on illness: chronic care taught from a biopsychosocial perspective with attention to cognitive functioning, pain and coping, and acute psychiatric illness and intellectual disability treated in the Critical Professional track.

Communication, collaboration, leadership and professionalism: four of the seven competencies the programme develops (communicator, collaborator, leader, professional) through the Professional and Personal Development track, small-group work, the skills lab and healthcare team participation, including communication with patients and their families, shared decision-making and medical leadership.

Clinical skills and patient contact: skills-lab training of physical examination, measuring blood pressure and administering injections on models, fellow students and simulated patients, patient contact in clinical settings from year 2, and participation in a healthcare team.

adjacentDirections.label: Public health, prevention and health promotion: the programme names prevention and health promotion as growing needs and as a medical responsibility, and the official future page lists the master's programmes Epidemiology, Health Promotion, Global Health and Governance and Leadership in European Public Health as follow-on directions.

questionsApplications.label: How health care responds to an ageing, culturally diverse population and to people whose health problems cannot be cured: the programme describes sociocultural diversity, population ageing and the support of patients with incurable conditions as developments that shape practice.
How doctors provide integrated, multidisciplinary care across disciplines, settings and stakeholders: the Integrated Care period of year 3 and the programme's emphasis on integrated care.

alternatives.concept: The strongest defensible UCR response to the Bachelor Geneeskunde at Maastricht University, a Dutch-language, numerus fixus three-year medical bachelor that trains students for the doctor's role through integrated care periods, skills-lab training and patient contact, with a Critical Professional line in epidemiology, statistics and ethics and law. UCR has no medical degree, clinical skills training, patient contact, healthcare placement or Dutch-language medical teaching, so this programme cannot reproduce the target's professional training or lead to the same qualification. It rebuilds the target's scientific knowledge base from UCR's biomedical science: the foundation of life and health, cell and molecular biology, biochemistry, human physiology, functional anatomy and neurobiology, followed by pharmacology, infection and immunity, mechanisms of disease and molecular pathology and genetics; epidemiology and public health, research methods, advanced statistics and systematic reviews for the scientific-thinking line; ethics and human rights for the ethics-and-law domain; and the biopsychosocial side of illness through brain and behaviour, health psychology, abnormal psychology, psychodiagnostics and lifespan development. Biomedical courses implement the target's knowledge of disease directly, whereas the psychology, ethics and law courses are complementary, and nothing in the programme substitutes for the clinical skills, patient contact or integrated care practice of the target.

The label names the biomedical science that dominates the programme, the psychology that supports the target's biopsychosocial perspective and the evidence-based research line, and it does not claim a medical curriculum, clinical training or a professional qualification that UCR does not offer.

alternatives.concept: The person-centred, psychological and professional side of the Bachelor Geneeskunde. Besides medical expertise, the target develops six further competencies, and the official programme names communication with patients and their families, shared decision-making, working with other professionals, leadership and professional development as core elements of patient care, in a setting of population ageing, sociocultural diversity and patients whose conditions cannot be cured. This alternative organises a UCR programme around those evidenced questions instead of the biomedical sciences: health psychology, abnormal psychology, psychodiagnostics and lifespan development with brain and behaviour and neurobiology; social psychology, persuasion and decision-making for how people communicate and choose; personal leadership, leadership communication, diversity management and organisational psychology for the collaborator and leader competencies; sociology and qualitative research for the experience of patients; ethics, human rights and AI ethics for professional responsibility; and epidemiology with a research-methods and statistics line for evidence. It requires no pretence of being a medical programme: it contains only a short biomedical foundation, no clinical skills or patient contact, and the leadership, communication and decision-making courses are general rather than medical, so they complement rather than replace the target's professional training.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 1 reconstructs the target's biomedical knowledge base, with eleven life-science and biomedical courses on the body in health and disease. Alternative 2 instead takes the target's person-centred competencies (communicator, collaborator, leader and professional, with shared decision-making, diversity and ageing) as its organising logic, evidenced by seven direct programme interests (5942, 5943, 5944, 5945, 5949, 5950 and 5955) and by the programme's own competency framework. It drops ten Alternative 1 courses (Molecular Cell Biology, Functional Anatomy, Human Physiology, Biochemistry, Pharmacology, Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease, Life Science Laboratory, Molecular Pathology & Genetics and Advanced Research Seminar) and adds ten courses that Alternative 1 does not contain (Social Psychology, Personal Leadership, Leadership Communication, Leadership & Diversity Management, Psychology of Organizations & Leadership, Persuasive Communication, Introduction to Sociology, Qualitative Research Methodology, AI Ethics and Behavioral Economics). The biomedical sciences are therefore replaced by psychology of interaction, leadership, communication, sociology and decision science. The programmes share 14 courses, including Personal & Professional Development, the brain-and-behaviour and clinical-psychology courses, epidemiology and the statistics courses, and each has 10 courses (75 EC) that the other lacks.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine in semester 1 precedes every other life-science and biomedical course (Molecular Cell Biology, Functional Anatomy, Human Physiology, Biochemistry, Pharmacology, Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease, Life Science Laboratory and Molecular Pathology & Genetics), and Introduction to Brain & Behavior in semester 1 precedes Higher Order Functions, Medical & Health Psychology, Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies, Abnormal Psychology, Lifespan Developmental Psychology and Advanced Research Seminar. The introductory courses come before the courses that build on them: Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) before Statistics & Experimental Methods (semester 3), which in turn precedes the Advanced Research Seminar on systematic reviews in semester 6; anatomy and cell biology (semester 2) and physiology and biochemistry (semester 3) come before Mechanisms of Disease and Infection & Immunity (semester 4) and before Pharmacology and Molecular Pathology & Genetics (semester 5). Epidemiology & Public Health, which is only offered in semesters 1 and 5, opens the programme.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible and production stopped at two. Alternative 1 owns eight generator-eligible rows that describe the target's own scientific core: 5937 on medicine and human health, 5938 on diagnosing illness, 5939 on treating and monitoring, 5940 and 5953 on preventing disease and population health problems (through Epidemiology & Public Health and Infection & Immunity), 5946 and 5947 on medical research and critical thinking about evidence, and 5948 on medical ethics. Alternative 2 is built on seven direct programme interests about the person-centred side of care (5942, 5943, 5944, 5945, 5949, 5950 and 5955) together with the programme's official competency framework; it supplies ten different courses and shares 14 with Alternative 1, so it passes the 30 EC / 4 course floor in both directions. A third alternative cannot be built. Clinical skills, physical examination, prognosis and patient contact (5951, 5952, 5956, with supporting rows 5957 to 5959) are the practical core of the target, but UCR offers no clinical skills training, patient contact or healthcare placement, and no course could implement the concept, so it is not feasible and no course is presented as a substitute. The population-health, prevention and advocacy direction (5941 and 5954) is evidenced by the programme and its master's pathways, but UCR has a single epidemiology course, already used in both alternatives, and no course on health promotion, health policy or public-health advocacy, so a programme would be an assortment of general social-science courses rather than an implementation of the concept.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Year 1 is an integrated competency-based year of four themed care periods, three longitudinal tracks, skills-lab training and electives assessed through one competency exam; no single UCR course addresses a component of this breadth, and the biomedical and psychology courses placed beside it each cover only a part of its knowledge base.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Year 2 is an integrated competency-based year of four themed care periods with patient contact in clinical settings, electives and healthcare team participation; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart for it, and the disease and pathology courses placed beside it address only the biomedical knowledge of its periods, without clinical practice.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Integrated Care is a 20-week clinical period in which students apply clinical reasoning and management across patients, settings and stakeholders, with Critical Appraisal of a Topic; the leadership, communication and organisational-psychology courses placed beside it address collaboration and decision-making in general, and no UCR course offers clinical integration or patient contact.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the minor is a 20-week open elective space in which students choose their own minor or study abroad; it is not a defined curriculum that any scheduled UCR course corresponds to.

blocks.title: Personal development and open elective space

comparator.text: Year 3: minor period of 20 weeks (a minor at FHML or another UM faculty, study abroad or a free-mover period)
comparator.note: Open elective space. The 20-week minor is a free choice among FHML minors, minors at other UM faculties and study abroad; the catalogue (s4) lists 30 EC for the FHML minor Leefstijlgeneeskunde and the minor period covers half of the 40-week year. No named minor is instantiated.

notes.text: The Bachelor Geneeskunde combines medical knowledge, skills-lab training, patient contact, healthcare team participation and the competencies of a doctor in a Dutch-language, numerus fixus programme. At UCR, students can approach human health and disease through fields such as biomedical science, life science, psychology and neuroscience, epidemiology and ethics. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than reproducing a full medical curriculum: UCR offers no clinical skills training, patient contact or healthcare placement.

The Bachelor Geneeskunde organises study around integrated, problem-based care periods in which knowledge, skills and attitude are learned through authentic doctor tasks, and it awards credit through annual competency exams rather than per course, so its four components are shown at the level at which the programme publishes its EC. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across individual 7.5-EC courses in biomedical science, psychology, epidemiology, ethics and law. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the target period by period.
